title: Ownership and Memory
subtitle: Understand Rust
description: Learn ownership rules, moves, stack and heap concepts, scope and how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 4: Ownership and Memory. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Ownership and Memory”. The goal is to understand Rust. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Ownership gives a program clear responsibility for a value and its lifetime. Make ownership transfers and copies deliberate so data is not unexpectedly shared or discarded.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Rust. Paste this snippet into the Rust editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 1: Ownership and Memory in practice
blocks.code: fn main() { let title = String::from("HTML"); let moved = title; println!("{moved}"); }

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Understand Rust. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A Rust String is moved into a new binding. What should the original binding normally be expected to do?
options: Remain usable for every operation without restriction.
Automatically become a global variable.
No longer be used as an owner unless the value was cloned or otherwise borrowed.
Become an integer.
blocks.explanation: A move transfers ownership, so the old binding is no longer valid for ordinary use.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A move transfers ownership, so the old binding is no longer valid for ordinary use.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A move transfers ownership, so the old binding is no longer valid for ordinary use.

blocks.question: A function only needs to inspect a value. What Rust mechanism generally communicates that no ownership transfer is needed?
options: Clone it repeatedly.
Use a mutable global.
Allocate a second value at random.
Borrow it through a reference.
blocks.explanation: Borrowing permits access without transferring ownership.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Borrowing permits access without transferring ownership.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Borrowing permits access without transferring ownership.

blocks.question: Why restrict simultaneous mutable references to the same data?
options: To prevent conflicting access and help avoid unsafe data races/aliasing bugs.
To make every value immutable forever.
To remove the need for types.
To force every variable to be copied.
blocks.explanation: Rust’s borrowing rules prevent conflicting mutable access and help guarantee memory safety.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Rust’s borrowing rules prevent conflicting mutable access and help guarantee memory safety.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Rust’s borrowing rules prevent conflicting mutable access and help guarantee memory safety.

blocks.question: A learner’s XP changes after every correct answer. Which design is easiest to maintain?
options: Repeat the current XP number in many places.
Store XP in one appropriately scoped variable and update it deliberately.
Use a different variable name for every update.
Convert XP to a text label before doing arithmetic.
blocks.explanation: One well-defined source of truth prevents values from drifting apart.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. One well-defined source of truth prevents values from drifting apart.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. One well-defined source of truth prevents values from drifting apart.

blocks.question: A setting must never be reassigned during the program. What should you choose?
options: A constant or immutable binding supported by the language.
A global variable that any function can change.
A string containing the setting name.
A loop that resets the value repeatedly.
blocks.explanation: Constants communicate intent and help prevent accidental reassignment.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Constants communicate intent and help prevent accidental reassignment.
